concepts.title: Perception of Sets

position.section_title: A Few Notes about Human Perception

concepts.one_liner: When an image is composed of one or a few distinct objects, we can easily pay attention to each of them individually.
concepts.content:
When an image is composed of one or a few distinct objects, we can easily pay attention to each of them individually. We can also count them in parallel, that is, we can tell if an image has one, two, three, or four elements, very quickly and the time it takes for us to say how many elements are in the display does not depend on the number of elements in the image. That is, if a display has only one element or four elements, we are equally fast at reporting that number (figures @fig-parallel_counting[a, b and c]).

(see figure: When looking at these images, we can count the number of circles at a glance if there are less than five circles. When an image has more than five items, we have to count them one by one.)

But something interesting happens when images are composed of more than five similarly looking elements. If we want to count them we need to look at all of them one by one, and the time to count them grows linearly with the number of elements in the image, as illustrated in @fig-parallel_counting.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept explains how humans perceive and count small numbers of objects quickly, but counting larger numbers requires serial attention, revealing limits of visual processing.
concepts.recap_md:
- Humans can quickly count up to four elements in an image in parallel.
- Counting more than five similar elements requires serial attention.
- Counting time grows linearly with the number of elements beyond five.

concepts.title: crowding

position.section_title: A Few Notes about Human Perception

concepts.one_liner: Crowding is a visual phenomenon where features of nearby objects get entangled, making it hard to perceive individual items in peripheral vision.
concepts.content:
@fig-crowding illustrates a curious visual phenomenon. Look at the central cross and try to read the letter on the left and right without moving your eyes.

(see figure: Crowding. If you look at the central cross, the letter R on the right can be recognized, however the letter B on the left is hard to read.)

You will notice that the letter R on the right can be recognized easily while the letter B on the left is hard to read. The reason cannot be due to the low resolution of peripheral vision as both letters are at the same distance from the fixation location. The explanation of this phenomena is due to something called **crowding** @Pell2007.

As the letter B is surrounded by other letters, the features of the three letters get entangled as if the pooling window for image features was larger than the three letters together. While you fixate the cross, as you pay attention to the location of the B, you will notice that the features of the three letters are mixed. It is easy to see that it is text, but it is hard to bind the features together to perceive the individual letters. The circles in @fig-crowding represent an approximation of the size of the visual regions over which visual features are pooled. Anything inside the region will suffer from crowding effects. Those regions are larger than what would be predicted by the loss of resolution due to the spacing between receptors in the periphery.

The main message here is for you to feel what it is to perceive what seems to be a statistical representation of the image features present in an image region.
concepts.motivation_md: Crowding explains why objects close together in peripheral vision become hard to recognize individually, revealing limits of feature integration in vision.
concepts.recap_md:
- Crowding occurs when features of nearby objects get mixed in peripheral vision.
- It impairs recognition of individual letters despite equal distance from fixation.
- Visual pooling regions are larger than receptor spacing predicts.

concepts.title: textons

position.section_title: A Few Notes about Human Perception

concepts.one_liner: Textures are analyzed in terms of statistical relationships between fundamental texture elements called textons.
concepts.content:
One of the first computational models of texture perception was due to Bela Julesz @Julesz1981. He proposed that textures are analyzed in terms of statistical relationships between fundamental texture elements that he called **textons**. It generally required a human to look at the texture in order to decide what those fundamental units were and his models were restricted to binary images formed by simple elements as shown in @fig-julez_texture.

(see figure: Texture discrimination using textons.)
concepts.motivation_md: Textons provide a foundational concept for modeling texture perception by identifying basic elements that compose textures.
concepts.recap_md:
- Textons are fundamental texture elements used to analyze textures.
- Bela Julesz introduced this computational model in 1981.
- Models were initially limited to binary images with simple elements.

concepts.title: Efros-Leung Texture Analysis and Synthesis Model

position.section_title: Efros-Leung Texture Analysis and Synthesis Model

concepts.one_liner: The Efros-Leung algorithm synthesizes texture by iteratively sampling pixels based on local neighborhood similarity in the input image.
concepts.content:
Nonparametric Markov random field image models, introduced earlier in chapter @sec-stat_image_models, define the probability distribution of a pixel as dependent on the neighborhood around the pixel. If the values of enough pixels surrounding a given pixel are specified, then the probability distribution of the given pixel is independent of the other pixels in the image. This image model can be used as a powerful texture synthesis model @Efros99.

As with other texture synthesis algorithms, the input to the Efros-Leung algorithm @Efros99 is an example of the texture to be synthesized, and the output is an image of more of that texture. It is an iterative algorithm as shown in @fig-sampling_efros_leung.

(see figure: In the Efros-Leung algorithm @Efros99)

At each iteration, we have synthesized pixels in the neighborhood of the pixel to be synthesized. We look through the input image for examples of similar configurations of pixel values as the current local neighborhood, having a sum of squared intensity differences from the local neighborhood lower than some threshold. We randomly select one of the matching instances and copy the value of the pixel into the pixel to be synthesized. This process is repeated for all pixels to be synthesized. It can be natural to synthesize the pixels in a raster-scan ordering. Image pixels without sufficient neighboring pixels for context can be randomly sampled from the input texture.

In this nonparametric model, the representation of a texture is the reference image itself. There is not a low-dimensional representation as in parametric texture models. The advantage is that no information is lost in this representation.

@fig-efros1 shows how the synthesized texture from the Efros-Leung algorithm @Efros99 changes as a function of the size of the context region. @fig-efros1a shows the source texture; @fig-efros1b shows how a very small context region (the grid of @fig-sampling_efros_leung) only covers a part of each circle and the synthesized texture doesn't show complete circles; @fig-efros1c shows how a larger context region yields a synthesized texture that maintains the circles, but not the regularity of their spacing; and @fig-efros1d shows how a still larger context region enforces all the spatial regularities of the input texture.

(see figure: A source texture image consisting of five white rings arranged in a quincunx pattern (four in the corners and one in the center) against a solid black background.)

(see figure: A black and white image showing a source texture of thin, white, squiggly lines and small loops scattered across a black background. The lines are irregular and vary in length and curvature...)

(see figure: A black and white texture image showing many small, white, ring-shaped circles scattered across a solid black background. The circles are roughly uniform in size but are distributed with some...)

(see figure: A source texture image consisting of a regular grid of white rings on a black background. The rings are arranged in a staggered, hexagonal-like pattern across the entire frame.)

Synthesized texture from the Efros-Leung algorithm @Efros99 as a function of size of the context region.

@fig-efrosresult shows additional image synthesis results. It is remarkable that such a simple model works so well. The results seem better than the ones shown in @fig-two_examples; however, note that there can still be artifacts (such as the very big leaf that appear in the output). Increasing the neighborhood size can remove those issues. Also, we can see that some elements of the reference texture might appear multiple times in the output texture. Removing repetitions requires decreasing the neighborhood size.

(see figure: Image synthesis results from the Efros-Leung algorithm. The small crops are used to synthesize the larger texture regions. Input images are 128 $\times$ 128 pixels, and the outputs are 256 $\times$...)

Embellishments have been developed that account for structures over scale @DeBonet98 or which are more efficient by operating on patches

concepts.title: generative adversarial networks
concepts.one_liner: Generative adversarial networks (GANs) create images matching learned statistics rather than hand-defined ones.
concepts.content: The Heeger-Bergen algorithm is also connected to generative adversarial networks (GANs), which we will encounter in @sec-generative_models-GANs. The objective of Heeger-Bergen is to make a texture that has the same histogram statistics as an exemplar. A GAN also makes images that have the same statistics as a set of exemplars; however, the statistics we seek to match are learned (by a so-called discriminator neural net) rather than hand-defined to be subband statistics.
concepts.motivation_md: GANs learn to generate images by matching statistical properties of exemplars through a discriminator network, enabling more flexible and powerful texture synthesis than fixed statistical methods.
concepts.recap_md:
- The Heeger-Bergen algorithm aims to match histogram statistics of a texture.
- GANs generate images matching learned statistics via a discriminator.
- GANs provide a learned alternative to hand-defined statistical matching.

concepts.title: relationship between texture models and human perception
concepts.one_liner: Texture models relate to human perception by aiming to reproduce image similarities relevant to humans.
concepts.content: There is an important relationship between texture models and human perception. One of the goals of many vision algorithms is to compute representations that reproduce image similarities relevant to humans. The representations might be the result of constraining the models to learn human preferences, or as a byproduct of unsupervised learning techniques that result in representations that correlate with human perception.
concepts.motivation_md: Texture models help create image representations that align with human perception, improving the relevance and effectiveness of vision algorithms.
concepts.recap_md:

- Vision algorithms compute representations aligned with human perception.
- These representations may result from learning human preferences or unsupervised methods.

concepts.title: Heeger-Bergen Texture Analysis and Synthesis
concepts.one_liner: The Heeger-Bergen texture synthesis method generates new random samples of a texture by matching filter response histograms across multiple scales and orientations.
concepts.content:
The statistical characteristics of image subbands allow for powerful image synthesis and denoising algorithms. The problem of texture synthesis is: given a reference texture, build a process that outputs images with new random samples of the same texture, as shown in @fig-analysis_heeger_bergen. Texture synthesis is important for many computer graphics applications and for studying useful texture representations for visual recognition.

An influential wavelet-based image synthesis algorithm is the Heeger-Bergen texture synthesis method published in 1995. David Heeger, inspired by Jim Bergen's talk about measuring filter response distributions for texture characterization, implemented the proposal using a steerable pyramid @Simoncelli95. Surprisingly, the first example worked well, leading to their influential paper @RG-Heeger-Bergen95.

Texture generation has two stages depicted in @fig-analysis_heeger_bergen: texture analysis extracts a texture representation, \(\theta\), from a reference texture; texture synthesis uses \(\theta\) to generate new random samples of the same texture. Defining "same texture" is difficult, but generally two textures are perceived as similar if they seem generated by the same physical process.

Texture synthesis is usually an iterative procedure starting with a random noise image and using \(\theta\) to produce improved images, as shown in @fig-heeger_bergen_iterations. The Heeger-Bergen approach decomposes the reference texture into multiple orientations and scales using oriented filters, such as a steerable pyramid with six orientations and three scales. The final texture representation concatenates the 18 subband histograms, the low-pass residual histogram, and the input image histogram (@fig-heegersubbands [a]).

The algorithm alternates matching the pixel intensity histogram of the image and matching histograms subband by subband in the transform domain. Histogram matching is implemented by a pointwise monotonic nonlinearity.

@fig-heegersubbands_histmatch shows histogram matching on one subband: the reference subband histogram has a Laplacian shape typical of natural images. Starting from white noise (Gaussian distribution), histogram matching modifies subband pixel values to match the reference histogram, making the noise subband sparser. This operation is done for all subbands.

@fig-heegersubbands (b) shows the result after applying histogram matching to all subbands and reconstructing the image. Then the output texture histogram is matched to the reference pixel histogram. Repeating these steps multiple times produces a synthesized texture that converges to a good approximation.

The results are often quite good for images like the triangles in @fig-analysis_heeger_bergen. However, correlations of filter responses across scales are not captured, so large-scale structures may be poorly depicted. For color images, principal component analysis (PCA) decorrelates color channels before applying texture analysis-synthesis independently to each channel, then projects back to the original color space. Running the algorithm for more than 15 iterations can degrade quality (@fig-two_examples).

Texture models using filter output statistics are precursors to diffusion models and share architectural features. The Heeger-Bergen model was one of the first successful filter-output-based texture representations. Later models introduced stronger statistical representations for higher quality textures @Portilla2000.

Parametric texture models represent a texture image with a small parameter vector, usually around 1,000 dimensions @Portilla2000.

concepts.recap_md:
- Heeger-Bergen method synthesizes textures by matching filter response histograms across scales and orientations.
- Texture analysis extracts a representation \(\theta\), used iteratively to refine noise into a texture sample.
- Histogram matching alternates between pixel and subband domains to converge on a synthesized texture.

key_passage.text: An influential wavelet-based image synthesis algorithm is the Heeger-Bergen texture synthesis method published in 1995, with the following origin story : David Heeger heard Jim Bergen give a talk at a human vision conference about representations for image texture. Bergen highlighted the value of measuring the mean-squared responses of filters applied to images for characterizing texture. He suggested that determining the full probability distribution of each filter's responses would be even more effective. He conjectured that if two textures produced the same distribution of filter responses for all filters, they would look identical to a human observer. Heeger disagreed and aimed to prove Bergen wrong by implementing the proposal using a steerable pyramid . To Heeger's surprise, the first example he tried worked very well, and this led to Heeger and Bergen's influential paper on texture synthesis .

concepts.title: histogram matching
concepts.one_liner: Histogram matching alternates between matching pixel intensity histograms and transform domain subband histograms to synthesize textures.
concepts.content:
The crux of the algorithm is to alternate matching the intensity domain pixel histogram of the image, then to transform the resulting image into the transform domain and enforce a match, subband by subband, of the image histograms there.

Histogram matching is implemented by a pointwise monotonic nonlinearity.

@fig-heegersubbands_histmatch shows how one of the subbands gets transformed by the histogram matching procedure. The histogram of the subband of the reference texture has the Laplacian shape typical of natural images. Most of the values of the output of the oriented filter are zero, and only near the triangle boundaries the values are non-zero. In the first iteration, the texture synthesis process starts with white noise (each pixel is sampled independently from a Gaussian distribution). The subband of the input noise has also a Gaussian distribution (as a linear combination of Gaussian random variables also follows a Gaussian distribution). Histogram matching modifies the values of each subband pixel (the histogram matching function is a pixelwise nonlinearity that depends on the current and target pixel histograms). After histogram matching, the noise subband looks sparser, with many values set to zero. The same operation is done for all the subbands in the steerable pyramid.

(see figure: Histogram matching for one of the subbands. The same operation is done for all the subbands independently.)
concepts.motivation_md: Histogram matching enforces statistical similarity between synthesized and reference textures both in pixel and transform domains, improving synthesis quality.
concepts.recap_md:
- Histogram matching alternates between pixel and subband domains.
- It uses a pointwise monotonic nonlinearity to adjust pixel values.
- Starting from noise, it progressively shapes subband histograms to match the reference.

concepts.title: Introduction
concepts.one_liner: A texture representation captures the statistics of similar-looking elements in an image, distinct from objects or surfaces.
concepts.content:
## Introduction

The visual world is made of objects (chairs, cars, tables), surfaces (walls, floor, ceiling), and stuff (wood, grass, water). This chapter is about seeing stuff @Adelson2001. How do we build image representations that can capture what makes wood different from a wall of bricks?

Representing textures is a task, similar to color perception, that is intimately related to human perception. A texture is a type of image that is composed by a set of similar looking elements. A texture representation contains information about the statistics of its constituent elements, but not about the elements individually.
concepts.motivation_md: Textures are important in vision and perception; representing them requires capturing statistical properties of their elements rather than individual details.
concepts.recap_md:
- Textures are made of similar-looking elements.
- Texture representation captures statistics, not individual elements.
- This is related to human perception of materials.

concepts.title: Texture synthesis can be solved by a trivial algorithm
concepts.one_liner: Texture synthesis can be trivially solved by cropping pieces from a large texture image, but this offers little insight into perception or texture representation.
concepts.content:
Texture synthesis can be solved by a trivial algorithm as shown in @fig-infinite_texture. But such an algorithm, although successful in practice, will give us little understanding on how human perception works and how to modify textures to create new ones. It will also not help us in understanding what representation can be useful to measure similarity between textures.

(see figure: The infinite texture generation algorithm. If we had access to a very large image of the texture we want to generate, we could just crop pieces from it to create new images.)
concepts.motivation_md: While trivial texture synthesis works, it does not explain human perception or help develop useful texture representations.
concepts.recap_md:
- Trivial texture synthesis crops from a large texture image.
- This method lacks insight into human perception.
- It does not aid in developing texture similarity measures.
